title: Estimation and uncertainty
description: Learn how to estimate software work honestly, communicate uncertainty clearly, and help your team make better planning decisions.

data.text: Estimation is one of the most misunderstood parts of software engineering. Management often treats estimates as promises, while engineers know that every estimate is built on assumptions that might change. As a senior engineer, your job is not to guess perfectly. It is to estimate honestly, communicate uncertainty, and help the team plan in a way that accounts for the unknown.

Uncertainty is not failure. It is information. A large, vague estimate says 'we do not know enough yet.' A small, precise estimate says 'we have explored this and understand the risks.' Both are useful, but only if you explain them clearly.

Estimates are wrong for many reasons: unknown unknowns, changing requirements, hidden dependencies, and optimism bias. The goal is not to eliminate error. It is to understand where the error is likely to come from and plan for it.

items: Unknown unknowns: we do not know what we do not know until we start building.
Optimism bias: engineers tend to assume the best-case path for their own work.
Scope creep: small changes accumulate into much larger work.
Dependencies: work that depends on another team is harder to estimate than solo work.

data.text: Instead of giving a single number, give three: the best case, the most likely case, and the worst case. This gives stakeholders a realistic range and makes the uncertainty visible.

data.title: Three-point estimate for a feature
data.code:
Feature: Add offline mode to the mobile app

Best case (if everything goes right):
  3 days - existing libraries work as expected

Most likely (accounting for some unknowns):
  5 days - we need to handle edge cases and test on real devices

Worst case (if we hit major issues):
  10 days - data sync conflicts require custom resolution logic

data.text: With this range, a manager can decide whether to plan around five days or to treat ten days as a contingency. That is far more useful than a single number that might be wrong.

The best way to improve an estimate is to reduce the unknowns. Before committing to a timeline, spend a small amount of time on discovery: read the relevant code, talk to the people who own the dependencies, and build a quick prototype if the approach is unproven.

data.title: Estimate with care
data.text: If someone pressures you for a number before you have done any discovery, it is okay to say: 'I can give you an estimate by end of day after I review the existing code.' A thoughtful estimate beats a confident guess every time.

data.title: Key takeaways
data.text: Estimation is a communication tool, not a prediction. Use ranges instead of single numbers, explain the sources of uncertainty, and invest in discovery before finalizing a timeline. Your goal is to help the team make informed decisions, not to be right.
